title: Burden sharing beyond budgets: Japan’s Official Security Assistance
gist: Japan's Official Security Assistance (OSA), launched in 2023 as the first Japanese aid channel permitted to equip foreign armed forces, more than doubled from 8.1bn yen (US$49m) in FY2025 to 18.1bn yen (US$116m) in FY2026. The argument is that despite a tiny budget, OSA grants of UAVs, patrol boats and coastal radar are strategically outsized in Pacific micro-states — Fiji's 2023 grant exceeded six times its own capital-purchase spend — and reframe deterrence as ISR and maritime-domain awareness rather than offensive weapons.

themes.theme: OSA breaks Japan's 70-year non-military aid taboo

insights.claim: Japan's Overseas Development Assistance, running since 1954, has been strictly designed for non-military purposes, and the Official Security Assistance programme launched in 2023 is the first channel allowed to assist foreign armed forces and their associated agencies.
insights.speaker: IISS
insights.so_what: A structural loosening of Japan's postwar constraints on security aid opens a new, growing government demand channel for defence-adjacent equipment exporters.
insights.quote: Unlike the ODA, the OSA can provide assistance to foreign armed forces and their associated agencies.
insights.locator: For decades, since it was announced in 1954

insights.claim: Japan's Official Security Assistance budget rose from 8.1 billion yen (about US$49 million) in FY2025 to 18.1 billion yen (about US$116 million) in FY2026, more than doubling in a single year.
insights.speaker: IISS
entities: Ministry of Foreign Affairs of Japan
insights.so_what: The doubling rate, not the absolute level, is the signal — track FY2027 appropriations as a read on how fast Tokyo is institutionalising security aid.
insights.quote: the budget was increased to 18.1bn yen (approximately US$116m) for FY2026
insights.locator: In 2023, changes in its security environment

insights.claim: The Official Security Assistance programme is led by Japan's Ministry of Foreign Affairs rather than its defence ministry, bridging Japanese diplomatic and military-security objectives in one instrument.
insights.speaker: IISS
entities: Ministry of Foreign Affairs of Japan
insights.so_what: Diplomatic ownership means OSA allocations follow foreign-policy priorities and partner requests, making recipient selection a leading indicator of Tokyo's strategic map.
insights.locator: Led by the Ministry of Foreign Affairs of Japan

themes.theme: Deterrence redefined as enabling capabilities, not weapons

insights.claim: Japan's security-assistance projects supply enabling capabilities — intelligence, surveillance and reconnaissance, maritime-domain awareness and communications — rather than offensive weapons, a deliberately broader framing than conventional war-fighting deterrence.
insights.speaker: IISS
insights.so_what: The addressable market created here is sensors, radar, UAVs and comms integration — not platforms or munitions.
insights.quote: Japan, however, appears to be taking a broader framing of deterrence
insights.locator: At a broader level, these initiatives do not depict the traditional strategic conversation

insights.claim: Approved Japanese security-assistance projects include grants for surveillance UAVs to Sri Lanka and Tonga in 2025 and a coastal radar system for Djibouti in 2024.
insights.speaker: IISS
insights.so_what: Tokyo's grant footprint now spans the Indian Ocean, the Pacific islands and the Horn of Africa — a wider geographic reach than Japan's formal alliance commitments.
insights.locator: For example, some of the approved projects include

insights.claim: Building recipient states' own capacity to analyse their regional security environment is treated as the precondition for them making effective contributions to collective regional defence.
insights.speaker: IISS
insights.so_what: Capability transfer aimed at decision-making rather than firepower implies long-tail service, training and data-sharing contracts.
insights.quote: Those capabilities improve a state’s ability to understand its security environment and make informed decisions.
insights.locator: Japan, however, appears to be taking a broader framing of deterrence

insights.claim: Japanese Minister of Defense Koizumi Shinjiro used the 2026 IISS Shangri-La Dialogue to frame the security-assistance programme as tangibly strengthening the deterrence and response capabilities of the region.
insights.speaker: IISS
insights.so_what: Ministerial-level framing at the region's main security forum indicates OSA is being positioned as an alliance-management card, not a niche aid line.
insights.quote: the aim of these initiatives is to tangibly strengthen deterrence and response capabilities of the region

insights.claim: Resilience through stronger defence capabilities and autonomy through sovereign security choices are the two themes recurring in Japanese Prime Minister Takaichi Sanae's recent remarks on the Indo-Pacific.
insights.speaker: IISS
insights.so_what: Tokyo is pitching an alternative to bloc alignment; expect Japanese security offers to be marketed on partner autonomy, competing with Chinese and US packages on framing as much as content.
insights.quote: These are the efforts to support each country to choose for itself, to defend itself and to contribute to regional stability

themes.theme: Modest budget, outsized marginal impact on micro-states

insights.claim: A US$116m annual security-assistance budget is too small to address the biggest threats facing the Indo-Pacific, which is the standing critique of Japan's programme.
insights.speaker: IISS
insights.so_what: Do not model OSA as a defence-procurement wave; its effect is concentrated and marginal, felt only in the smallest recipient budgets.
insights.quote: A US$116m annual budget has limitations and will not address some of the biggest threats facing the Indo-Pacific.
insights.locator: Modest means, big impact and small states

insights.claim: Japan's roughly 400 million yen 2023 grant to Fiji for patrol boats and underwater cameras was worth over six times Fiji's entire capital-purchase expenditure that year.
insights.speaker: IISS
insights.so_what: In Pacific micro-states a few hundred million yen buys structural influence; the leverage per dollar is orders of magnitude above great-power defence spending.
insights.quote: The value was over six times Fiji’s expenditure for capital purchase in 2023.

insights.claim: Japan's 2025 security-assistance grants to Papua New Guinea equalled 50% of the Papua New Guinea defence ministry's plant, machinery and equipment budget for that year.
insights.speaker: IISS
insights.so_what: Tokyo is becoming a swing funder of Pacific island military recapitalisation — a direct contest with Chinese security offers in the same states.
insights.locator: Similarly, the value of grants to Papua New Guinea in 2025

insights.claim: In 2026 Japan launched its first trilateral security-assistance project, partnering with Australia to redevelop a battalion headquarters in Fiji, and is likely to pursue similar arrangements with the other Quad partners, the US and India.
insights.speaker: IISS
insights.so_what: Watch for Quad-branded co-funded infrastructure in the Pacific as the practical vehicle for minilateral security cooperation.
insights.quote: the OSA announced its first trilateral project with Australia to redevelop a battalion headquarters in Fiji

themes.theme: Burden sharing measured beyond defence spending

insights.claim: Japan's security assistance should be read alongside its gradual relaxation of defence export restrictions and defence-industrial cooperation, including the prospective export of Mogami-class frigates, as components of one wider strategic shift.
insights.speaker: IISS
insights.so_what: Japanese defence-industrial exports and grant aid are moving together — a re-rating case for Japanese shipbuilders and defence primes tied to policy liberalisation rather than domestic budget alone.
insights.quote: including the prospective export of Mogami-class frigates

insights.claim: As Washington presses allies to shoulder more regional security responsibility, burden sharing will increasingly be judged by a state's ability to contribute to regional stability rather than by its defence-spending ratio alone.
insights.speaker: IISS
insights.so_what: A qualitative burden-sharing metric gives Japan an alternative to headline GDP-share spending targets — relevant to how US pressure on allied budgets resolves.
insights.quote: burden sharing will increasingly be measured not only by defence spending but also by states’ ability to contribute meaningfully to regional stability
insights.locator: As the US continues to ask allies and partners

insights.claim: Japan's decisive contribution to Indo-Pacific security may prove to be strengthening regional autonomy in ways that make collective deterrence more credible and sustainable, rather than the scale of its assistance.
insights.speaker: IISS
insights.so_what: If small enabling grants are the model, the Indo-Pacific security architecture consolidates around distributed awareness networks rather than a single hub-and-spoke build-out.
insights.quote: Rather than the scale of its assistance, what may yet define Japan’s contribution is its ability to strengthen regional autonomy in ways that make collective deterrence more credible and more sustainable.
